<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|656|SPHERICAL HARMONICS|}}</noinclude>From this form it can be shown that

{{block center|<math>\text{Q}_n(\mu) = \frac{1}{2}\text{P}_n(\mu)\log\frac{\mu+1}{\mu-1} - \text{W}_{n-1}(\mu),</math>}}

where <math>\text{W}_{n-1}(\mu)</math> is a rational integral function of degree <math>n-1</math> in <math>\mu</math>; it can be shown that this form is in agreement with the definition of <math>\text{Q}_n(\mu)</math> by series, for the case mod <math>\mu > 1</math>. In case mod <math>\mu < 1</math> it is convenient to use the symbol <math>\text{Q}_n(\mu)</math> for

{{block center|<math>\frac{1}{2}\text{P}_n(\mu)\log\frac{1+\mu}{1-\mu} - \text{W}_{n-1}(\mu),</math>}}

which is real when <math>\mu</math> is real and between <math>\pm 1</math>, the function <math>\text{Q}_n(\mu)</math> in this case is not the analytical continuation of the function <math>\text{Q}_n(\mu)</math> for mod <math>\mu > 1</math>, but differs from it by an imaginary multiple of <math>\text{P}_n(\mu)</math>. It will be observed that <math>\text{Q}_n(1)</math>, <math>\text{Q}_n(-1)</math> are infinite, and <math>\text{Q}_n(\infty) = 0</math>. The function <math>\text{W}_{n-1}(\mu)</math> has been expressed by Christoffel in the form

{{block center|<math>\frac{2n-1}{1.n}\text{P}_{n-1}(\mu) + \frac{2n-5}{3.n-1}\text{P}_{n-3}(\mu) + \frac{2n-9}{5.n-2}\text{P}_{n-5}(\mu) + \dots,</math>}}

and it can also be expressed in the form

{{block center|<math>\frac{1}{n}\text{P}_0(\mu)\text{P}_{n-1}(\mu) + \frac{1}{n-1}\text{P}_1(\mu)\text{P}_{n-2}(\mu) + \dots + \text{P}_{n-1}(\mu)\text{P}_0(\mu).</math>}}

It can easily be shown that the formula (28) is equivalent to

{{block center|<math>\text{Q}_n(\mu) = 2^n n!\int_\mu^\infty\int_\mu^\infty\dots\int_\mu^\infty\frac{(d\mu)^{\ n+1}}{(\mu^2-1)^{n+1}}</math>}} which is analogous to Rodrigue's expression for <math>\text{P}_n(\mu)</math>.

Another expression of a similar character is
{{block center|<math>\text{Q}_n(\mu) = (-1)^n \frac{2^n n!}{(2n)!} \frac{d^n}{d\mu^n} \left\{ (\mu^2-1)^n \int_\mu^\infty \frac{d\mu}{(\mu^2-1)^{n+1}} \right\}</math>.}}
It can be shown that under the condition mod <math>\{u-\sqrt{(u^2-1)}\} > \text{mod}\ \{\mu-\sqrt{(\mu^2-1)}\}</math>, the function <math>1/(\mu-u)</math> can be expanded in the form <math>\Sigma(2n+1)\text{P}_n(u)\text{Q}_n(u)</math>; this expansion is connected with the definite integral formula for <math>\text{Q}_n(\mu)</math> which was used by F. Neumann as a definition of the function <math>\text{Q}_n(\mu)</math>, this is
{{block center|<math>\text{Q}_n(\mu) = \frac{1}{2}\int_{-1}^1 \frac{\text{P}_n(u)}{\mu-u}du</math>,}}
which holds for all values of <math>\mu</math> which are not real and between <math>\pm 1</math>.

From Neumann's integral can be deduced the formula
{{block center|<math>\text{Q}_n(\mu) = \int_1^\infty \frac{d\psi}{\{\mu+\sqrt{(\mu^2-1)}.\cosh\psi\}^{n+1}}</math>,}}
which holds for all values of <math>\mu</math> which are not real and between <math>\pm 1</math>, provided the sign of <math>\sqrt{(\mu^2-1)}</math> is properly chosen; when <math>\mu</math> is real and greater than <math>1</math>, <math>\sqrt{(\mu^2-1)}</math> has its positive value.

By means of the substitution.
{{block center|<math>\{\mu+\sqrt{(\mu^2-1)}.\cosh\psi\}\{\mu-\sqrt{(\mu^2-1)}.\cosh\chi\} = 1</math>,}}
the above integral becomes
{{block center|<math>\text{Q}_n(\mu) = \int_0^{\chi_0} \{\mu-\sqrt{(\mu^2-1)}.\cosh\chi\}^n d\chi</math>, where <math>\chi_0 = \frac{1}{2}\log_e\frac{\mu+1}{\mu-1}</math>.}}
This formula gives a simple means of calculating <math>\text{Q}_n(\mu)</math> for small values of <math>n</math>; thus {{block center|<math>\text{Q}_0(\mu) = \int_0^{\chi_0} d\chi = \frac{1}{2}\log_e\frac{\mu+1}{\mu-1}.</math>}}

{{block center|<math>\text{Q}_1(\mu) = \mu\chi_0 - \sqrt{(\mu^2-1)}\,.\,\sinh\,\chi_0 = \mu\,.\,\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{\mu+1}{\mu-1} - 1.</math>}}

Neumann's integral affords a means of establishing a relation between successive <math>\text{Q}</math> functions, thus

{{block center|<math>n\text{Q}_n - (2n-1)\mu\text{Q}_{n-1} + (n-1)\text{Q}_{n-2}</math>}}

{{block center|<math>= \frac{1}{2}\int_{-1}^1 \frac{n\text{P}_n(u) + (n-1)\text{P}_{n-2}(u) - (2n-1)}{\mu - u}\mu\text{P}_{n-1}(u)du</math>}}

{{block center|<math>= -\frac{1}{2}\int_{-1}^1 (2n-1)\text{P}_{n-1}(u) = 0.</math>}}

Again, it may similarly be proved that

{{block center|<math>\frac{d\text{Q}_{n+1}}{d\mu} - \frac{d\text{Q}_{n-1}}{d\mu} = (2n+1)\text{Q}_n.</math>}}

19. ''Legendre Associated Functions.''—Returning to the equation (26) satisfied by <math>u^m_n</math> the factor in the normal forms <math>{r^n \atop r^{-n-1}}\,{\cos \atop \sin}\,m\phi\,.\,u^m_n</math>, we shall consider the case in which <math>n</math>, <math>m</math> are positive integers, and <math>n \geqq m</math>. Let <math>u = (\mu^2-1)^{\frac{1}{2}m}v</math>, then it will be found that <math>v</math> satisfies the equation

{{block center|<math>(1-\mu^2)\frac{d^2v}{d\mu^2} - 2(m+1)\mu\frac{dv}{d\mu} + (n-m)(n+m+1)v = 0.</math>}}

If, in Legendre's equation, we differentiate <math>m</math> times, we find

{{block center|<math>(1-\mu^2)\frac{d^{m+2}u}{d\mu^{m+2}}-2(m+1)\mu\frac{d^{m+1}u}{d\mu^{m+1}}+(n-m)(n+m+1)\frac{d^mu}{d\mu^m}=0;</math>}}

it follows that <math>v=\frac{d^mu}{d\mu^m}</math>, hence <math>u^m_n=(\mu^2-1)^{\frac{1}{2}m}\frac{d^mu}{d\mu^m}</math>.

The complete solution of (26) is therefore

{{block center|<math>u=(\mu^2-1)^{\frac{1}{2}m}\left\{\text{A}\frac{d^m\text{P}_n(\mu)}{d\mu^m}+\text{B}\frac{d^m\text{Q}_n(\mu)}{d\mu^m}\right\};</math>}}

when <math>\mu</math> is real and lies between <math>\pm1</math>, the two functions

{{block center|<math>(1-\mu^2)^{\frac{1}{2}m}\frac{d^m\text{P}_n(\mu)}{d\mu^m},(1-\mu^2)^{\frac{1}{2}m}\frac{d^m\text{Q}_n(\mu)}{d\mu^m}</math>}}

are called Legendre's associated functions of degree <math>n</math>, and order <math>m</math>, of the first and second kinds respectively. When <math>\mu</math> is not real and between <math>\pm1</math>, the same names are given to the two functions

{{block center|<math>(\mu^2-1)^{\frac{1}{2}m}\frac{d^m\text{P}_n(\mu)}{d\mu^m},\ (\mu^2-1)^{\frac{1}{2}m}\frac{d^m\text{Q}_n(\nu)}{d\mu^m};</math>}}

in either case the functions may be denoted by <math>\text{P}^m_n(\mu)</math>, <math>\text{Q}^m_n(\mu)</math>.

It can be shown that, when <math>\mu</math> is real and between <math>\pm1</math>

{{block center|<math>\text{P}^m_n(\mu)=\frac{(-1)^m}{2^n(n-m)!}\left(\frac{1+\mu}{1-\mu}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}m}\frac{d^n}{d\mu^n}\{(\mu-1)^{n+m}(\mu+1)^{n-m}\}</math>}}

{{block center|<math>=\frac{1}{2^n(n-m)!}\left(\frac{1-\mu}{1+\mu}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}m}\frac{d^n}{d\mu^n}\{(\mu-1)^{n-m}(\mu+1)^{n+m}\}.</math>}}

In the same case, we find

{{block center|<math>\text{P}^{m+2}_n(\cos\theta)-2(m+1)\cot\theta\,\text{P}^{m+1}_n(\cos\theta)</math>}}

{{block center|<math>+(n-m)(n+m+1)\text{P}^m_n(\cos\theta)=0, (n-m+2)\text{P}^m_{n+2}(\cos\theta)-(2n+3)\mu\text{P}^m_{n+1}(\cos\theta)</math>}}
{{block center|<math>+(n+m+1)\text{P}^m_n(\cos\theta)=0.</math>}}

20. ''Bessel's Functions.''—If we take for three orthogonal systems of surfaces a system of parallel planes, a system of co-axial circular cylinders perpendicular to the planes, and a system of planes through the axis of the cylinders, the parameters are <math>z</math>, <math>\rho</math>, <math>\phi</math>, the cylindrical co-ordinates; in that case <math>\text{H}_1=1</math>, <math>\text{H}_2=1</math>, <math>\text{H}_3=1/\rho</math>, and the equation (25) becomes
{{block center|<math>\frac{\partial^2\text{V}}{\partial z^2}+\frac{\partial^2\text{V}}{\partial\rho^2}+\frac{1}{\rho}\frac{\partial\text{V}}{\partial\rho}+\frac{1}{\rho^2}\frac{\partial^2\text{V}}{\partial\phi^2}=0.</math>}}

To find the normal functions which satisfy this equation, we put <math>\text{V}=\text{ZR}\Phi</math>, when <math>\text{Z}</math> is a function of <math>z</math> only, <math>\text{R}</math> of <math>\rho</math> only, and <math>\Phi</math> of <math>\phi</math>, the equation then becomes
{{block center|<math>\frac{1}{\text{Z}}\frac{d^2\text{Z}}{dz^2}+\frac{1}{\text{R}}\left(\frac{d^2\text{R}}{d\rho^2}+\frac{1}{\rho}\frac{d\text{R}}{d\rho}\right)+\frac{1}{\rho^2}\frac{1}{\Phi}\frac{d^2\Phi}{d\phi^2}=0.</math>}}
That this may be satisfied we must have <math>\frac{1}{\text{Z}}\frac{d^2\text{Z}}{dz^2}</math> constant, say <math>=k^2</math>, <math>\frac{1}{\text{Z}}\frac{d^2\text{Z}}{dz^2}</math> constant, say <math>=-m^2</math>, and <math>\text{R}</math>, for which we write <math>u</math>, must satisfy the differential equation
{{block center|<math>\frac{d^2u}{d\rho^2}+\frac{1}{\rho}\frac{du}{d\rho}+\left(k^2-\frac{m^2}{\rho^2}\right)u=0,</math>}}
it follows that the normal forms are <math>e^{\pm kz}{}^{\cos}_{\sin}m\phi\,.\,u(k\rho)</math>, where <math>u(\rho)</math> satisfies the equation
{{block center|<math>\frac{d^2u}{d\rho^2}+\frac{1}{\rho}\frac{du}{d\rho}+\left(1-\frac{m^2}{\rho^2}\right)u=0.</math> (29)}} This is known as Bessel's equation of order <math>m</math>; the particular case
{{block center|<math>\frac{d^2u}{d\rho^2}+\frac{1}{\rho}\,\frac{du}{d\rho}+u=0,</math> (30)}}
corresponding to <math>m=0</math>, is known as Bessel's equation.

If we solve the equation (29) in series, we find by the usual process that it is satisfied by the series
{{block center|<math>\rho^m\left\{1-\frac{\rho^2}{2.2m+2}+\frac{\rho^4}{2.4.2m+2.2m+4}-\dots\right\};</math>}}
the expression
{{block center|<math>\frac{\rho^m}{2^m\Pi(m)}\left\{1-\frac{\rho^2}{2.2m+2}+\frac{\rho^4}{2.4.2m+2.2m+4}-\dots\right\}</math>}}
or
{{block center|<math>\sum_{n=0,}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n\rho^{m+2n}}{2^{m+2n}\Pi(m+n)\Pi(n)}</math>}}
is denoted by <math>\text{J}_m(\rho)</math>.

When <math>m=0</math>, the solution
{{block center|<math>1-\frac{\rho^2}{2^2}+\frac{\rho^4}{2^2.4^2}-\dots</math>}}
of the equation (30) is denoted by <math>\text{J}_0(\rho)</math> or by <math>\text{J}(\rho)</math>.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
